core_principles.text: A systemic corrective exercise program focusing on hip and ankle strength and flexibility can decrease 2- and 3-dimensional knee valgus during a double-legged squat.
Increasing ankle-dorsiflexion flexibility can help reduce medial knee displacement and dynamic knee valgus during a squat.

common_mistakes.text: Allowing the knees to cave inward (medial knee displacement or dynamic knee valgus) during a double-legged squat.
Squatting with restricted ankle-dorsiflexion range of motion, which is associated with increased knee valgus.

specific_findings.text: In a randomized controlled trial of 32 participants, a 10-session directed exercise intervention over 2 to 3 weeks significantly decreased medial knee displacement from 20% to 50% of the double-legged squat phase (P = .02).
The 10-session exercise intervention significantly improved 3D knee valgus from 30% to 50% of the squat phase (P = .001).
Ankle-dorsiflexion range of motion with the knee extended significantly increased in the intervention group (P = .009) following the corrective exercise program.

consequences.text: Knee valgus is believed to be a major contributor to noncontact anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injuries.
A lack of femoral control during squatting can result in excessive femoral adduction and internal rotation, which stresses the anterior cruciate ligament (ACL).

core_principles.text: Placing a 2-inch heel lift under the heels during a squat can alleviate ankle dorsiflexion restrictions caused by tight gastrocnemius and soleus muscles, thereby normalizing knee alignment.
A comprehensive corrective strategy for knee valgus should target both the hip joints proximal and ankle joints distal to the knee.
A standard screening setup for the double-legged squat involves standing with feet shoulder-width apart, toes pointed straight ahead, and hands overhead with elbows locked.

common_mistakes.text: Allowing the knees to cave inward, known as dynamic knee valgus or medial knee displacement, during the descent or ascent of a squat.
Squatting with restricted ankle dorsiflexion due to tightness in the gastrocnemius and soleus muscles.

specific_findings.text: Visual knee valgus is clinically defined during a double-legged squat screening when the midpoint of the patella passes medial to the great toe in 3 out of 5 trials.
The double-legged squat screening protocol utilizes a 2-inch (5.08-cm) heel lift to differentiate between ankle and hip-muscle imbalances as the primary contributor to dynamic knee valgus.

consequences.text: Limited ankle dorsiflexion forces biomechanical compensations including increased subtalar pronation, tibial abduction, and internal rotation, which contribute to knee valgus.
Excessive knee valgus and poor movement quality during squatting or landing tasks are theorized to increase the overall risk of lower extremity injury.

core_principles.text: Knee valgus can be screened in real time using a categorical yes-no grading system based on whether the patella passes medial to the great toe during the squat.

common_mistakes.text: Allowing the patella to pass medial to the great toe during a squat is a sign of excessive knee valgus.

specific_findings.text: A study of 32 volunteers classified participants as having excessive visual knee valgus if the patella passed medial to the great toe in 3 of 5 squats.

core_principles.text: Keep the knees aligned over the toes during squatting and integrative exercises to maintain proper lower extremity alignment.

Inhibit overactive muscles such as the gastrocnemius, lateral hamstring, and adductors by foam rolling each muscle for 2 minutes, allowing the roller to sit for 30 seconds over tight or painful areas.
Lengthen tight muscles including the gastrocnemius, soleus, lateral hamstring, and adductors using static stretches held for 2 sets of 30 seconds.
Strengthen weak muscles such as the medial gastrocnemius, medial hamstring, and tibialis posterior using a slow, controlled tempo.

common_mistakes.text: Allowing the knees to displace medially (medial knee displacement or valgus) during the descent phase of the squat.

specific_findings.text: The corrective exercise intervention consisted of 10 sessions over a 3-week period, focusing on 5 exercises for hip musculature and 5 for ankle musculature.
Strengthening repetitions in the corrective protocol were performed at a controlled 7-count tempo: 1 count concentric, 2 counts isometric, and 4 counts eccentric.

The study identified the gastrocnemius, lateral hamstring, and adductors as overactive muscles, and the medial gastrocnemius, medial hamstring, and tibialis posterior as weak muscles contributing to medial knee displacement.

core_principles.text: A systematic corrective exercise program focusing on ankle mobility and lower limb strengthening can successfully reduce medial knee displacement and 3D knee valgus during a double-leg squat.
Increasing ankle-dorsiflexion range of motion with the knee extended is associated with a reduction in frontal-plane knee motion during a squat.

common_mistakes.text: Allowing the knees to collapse or displace medially (medial knee displacement and 3D knee valgus) during the squat phase, particularly from 20% to 50% of the descent.

specific_findings.text: The intervention group reduced 3D knee-valgus angle (P = .001, F1,150 = 4.43) from 30% to 50% of the squat phase and medial knee displacement (F1,150 = 3.4, P = .02) from 20% to 50% of the squat phase.
Ankle dorsiflexion with the knee extended increased in the intervention group (t1,30 = 2.8, P = .009, d = 0.77), whereas ankle dorsiflexion with the knee flexed did not (t1,30 = 0.47, P = .64).

core_principles.text: Ankle dorsiflexion restrictions play a significant role in causing knee valgus (medial knee displacement) during a double-leg squat.

Using a heel lift can temporarily correct excessive medial knee displacement during a squat by placing the ankle in a plantar-flexed position, which increases the available range of ankle-dorsiflexion motion during the descent.
To permanently improve knee valgus, training programs should incorporate targeted ankle strength and flexibility exercises.
Resolving ankle mobility restrictions allows the knees to track properly over the toes during the descent phase of a squat.

common_mistakes.text: Allowing the knees to cave inward (medial knee displacement or knee valgus) during a squat.
Squatting with restricted ankle dorsiflexion or tight gastrocnemius muscles, which limits ankle range of motion.

specific_findings.text: Traditional 3D assessment of knee-valgus angle and moment has been shown to predict noncontact ACL injury in females with 78% sensitivity and 73% specificity.
The study's ankle-focused intervention significantly reduced 3D knee valgus by 5 degrees, representing a 64% reduction.
The intervention successfully reduced medial knee displacement (MKD) by an average of 4 cm.
An MKD assessment combined with tibia length, knee-flexion motion, mass, and quadriceps-to-hamstrings strength ratio predicted high knee-abduction moment with 77% sensitivity and 71% specificity.

consequences.text: Tight plantar flexors increase ankle joint stiffness, forcing compensations such as increased foot pronation and proximal medial knee displacement (knee valgus) to reach the required squat depth.
Gastrocnemius tightness can result in excessive rearfoot pronation and flat foot.
Allowing medial knee displacement (knee valgus) increases knee-abduction moments, which is a key risk factor for noncontact ACL injuries.

core_principles.text: Interventions to improve knee valgus should include ankle exercises to address restricted ankle motion as part of a comprehensive program.
Maintaining adequate hip-abduction and hip-extension strength is important to control dynamic lower extremity motion and prevent excessive femoral adduction and internal rotation.

common_mistakes.text: Allowing the knees to cave inward (medial knee displacement or dynamic knee valgus) during squatting movements.
Squatting with restricted ankle motion, which can limit sagittal-plane motion and contribute to medial knee displacement.
Squatting with weak hip abductors and hip extensors, which can lead to excessive femoral adduction and internal rotation.

specific_findings.text: A female with 8.2 cm of medial knee displacement (MKD) has a 74% chance of demonstrating a high knee-abduction moment, whereas a 4-cm reduction in MKD reduces this chance to less than 40%.
Individuals classified as having poor single-legged squat technique had 29% less hip-abduction torque compared with those with good technique.

consequences.text: Weakness of the hip extensors and hip abductors may result in excessive femoral adduction and internal rotation, which are components of medial knee displacement.
Excessive medial knee displacement increases the likelihood of demonstrating a high knee-abduction moment.
